notes.intro: Thatha loves puzzles. Every evening he gives Anu a number riddle: 'Can five odd numbers add up to 20?' 'Can you fill a grid so that every line has the same sum?' You use odd and even numbers, magic squares and a famous Indian number pattern to solve puzzles without long calculations.
before: add numbers quickly in your head

lessons.title: Numbers can tell us things
lessons.story: Ten children stand in a line. Each child says how many children in front of them are taller. The first child always says 0. From these numbers alone, Anu can find the tallest child!
text: The tallest child sees nobody taller in front, so says 0. A child who says 0 is taller than everyone in front.
A similar idea: in a grid of numbers, a supercell is a number that is bigger than all its neighbours (left, right, above, below). The smallest number in a grid can never be a supercell.

picture.caption: Gold cells are supercells: each is bigger than all its neighbours.

think.question: Is 18 (centre) a supercell in this grid?
think.answer: No. Its neighbours 45, 30, 52 and 25 are bigger.

lessons.aha: Numbers can carry information. Read what a number says about its position or neighbours.

lessons.title: Odd and even: the pairing test
lessons.story: Anu has 7 chocolates and wants to share them with her brother so that each gets the same number. She makes pairs, and one chocolate is left over.
text: A number is even if its objects can be put into pairs with nothing left over. It is odd if exactly one object is left. 6 = 3 pairs (even). 7 = 3 pairs + 1 (odd).
Add two odd numbers: the two left-over objects make a new pair, so odd + odd = even. Odd + even leaves one object alone, so it is odd. Even + even is even.

picture.caption: The parity rules come from pairing objects.

think.question: Is 23 + 45 + 67 + 89 odd or even?
think.answer: Four odd numbers make two pairs of 'left-overs', so the sum is even (it is 224).

lessons.aha: Count the odd numbers in a sum. An even count of odd numbers gives an even sum. An odd count gives an odd sum.

lessons.title: Proving 'impossible' with parity
lessons.story: Thatha asks, 'Can you choose 3 numbers from 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 that add up to 20?' Anu tries for ten minutes and fails. Thatha says, 'You can stop. It is impossible, and I can prove it in one line.'
text: All five numbers are odd. Three odd numbers give an odd sum, because the count of odd numbers (3) is odd. 20 is even. An odd sum can never be 20.
This is the power of parity: you do not need to try every case. One rule settles the question.

picture.caption: Three odd numbers: two 'left-over' ones pair up, and one is always alone, so the sum is odd.

think.question: Can 7 odd numbers add up to 50?
think.answer: No. 7 odd numbers give an odd sum, and 50 is even.

lessons.aha: To show that something is impossible, look for an odd/even mismatch.

lessons.title: Parity of expressions
lessons.story: Ravi says, 'n × (n + 1) is always even.' Anu tries 3 × 4 = 12, 6 × 7 = 42, 9 × 10 = 90. It works! But why?
text: 2n is always even (it is 2 times a number), and 2n + 1 is always odd. So any even number can be written 2n, and any odd number 2n + 1.
n and n + 1 are consecutive numbers, so one of them is even. An even number times anything is even, so n(n + 1) is always even.
In a grid: a rectangle of a × b small squares has an odd number of squares only if both a and b are odd.

picture.caption: Parity of expressions.

think.question: Is n² + n always even?

lessons.aha: Even numbers have the form 2n, odd numbers 2n + 1. Use these forms to prove parity facts.

lessons.title: Adding odd numbers makes squares
lessons.story: Anu arranges buttons. She puts 1 button, then adds 3 around it in an L shape, then 5 more, then 7 more. Each time she gets a perfect square!
text: Each new odd number is an L-shaped border that makes the square one size bigger. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n = n².

picture.caption: The gold 3 × 3 square plus a blue L of 7 makes a 4 × 4 square.

think.question: Find 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 19 without adding.
think.answer: There are 10 odd numbers, so the sum is 10² = 100.

lessons.aha: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n².

lessons.title: Magic squares
lessons.story: Thatha draws a 3 × 3 grid. 'Put the numbers 1 to 9 in it, so that every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same number.'
text: First find the magic sum. 1 + 2 + … + 9 = 45. The 3 rows share this total equally, so each row adds to 45 ÷ 3 = 15.

The centre number is used by 4 lines (a row, a column and two diagonals). It must be 5, the middle number. Then pair the other numbers around it: 2 and 8, 4 and 6, 1 and 9, 3 and 7 (each pair adds to 10).

picture.caption: Every row, column and diagonal adds to 15. The centre is 5.

think.question: If you add 1 to every number of this magic square, what is the new magic sum?
think.answer: Each line has 3 numbers, so the sum grows by 3: 18.

lessons.aha: Magic sum = total of all numbers ÷ number of rows. In a 1–9 square, the centre is always 5.

lessons.title: A famous 4 × 4 magic square
lessons.story: At the Parshvanath temple in Khajuraho, carved about 1,000 years ago, there is a 4 × 4 square of numbers. Every row, column and diagonal adds up to 34!
text: It uses the numbers 1 to 16. Their total is 136, and there are 4 rows, so the magic sum is 136 ÷ 4 = 34. This square is called the Chautisa Yantra ('chautis' means 34).
In 1356, the Indian mathematician Narayana Pandita wrote methods to make magic squares of many sizes. Magic squares appear in art and culture all over the world.

picture.caption: The Chautisa Yantra: every row, column and diagonal adds to 34.

think.question: Check the gold diagonal of the Chautisa Yantra.

lessons.aha: Magic sum = total of all numbers ÷ number of rows. For 1 to 16 it is 34.

lessons.title: Virahānka's rhythm numbers
lessons.story: More than 1,300 years ago, the scholar Virahānka asked: how many rhythms of n beats can you make from short syllables (1 beat) and long syllables (2 beats)?
text: 1 beat: only S (1 way). 2 beats: SS or L (2 ways). 3 beats: SSS, SL, LS (3 ways). 4 beats: 5 ways.

Every rhythm ends with S or with L. If it ends with S, the rest is a rhythm of (n − 1) beats. If it ends with L, the rest is a rhythm of (n − 2) beats. So each count is the sum of the two counts before it: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …

picture.caption: Each number is the sum of the two before it.

think.question: How many rhythms of 6 beats are there?

lessons.aha: Virahānka numbers: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … Each number is the sum of the previous two.

lessons.title: Digits in disguise
lessons.story: Thatha writes a puzzle: A + A + A = BA. Each letter is one digit, and BA is a 2-digit number. 'Find A and B.'
text: BA means 10B + A. So 3A = 10B + A, which gives 2A = 10B, so A = 5B.
A is one digit, so B = 1 and A = 5. Check: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. ✓ Use place value and small cases to break the code.

picture.caption: A + A + A = BA. The answer: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.

think.question: AB + BA = 99 and A − B = 1. Find AB.

lessons.aha: Write each 'word' with place value (BA = 10B + A), then solve.

notes.intro: Anu and Ravi make triangles with sticks for a school project. Sometimes the sticks fit, and sometimes they just cannot meet. 'Why?' asks Ravi.
before: use a ruler, compasses and a protractor

lessons.title: Will the sticks meet?
lessons.story: Ravi takes sticks of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm. He lays the 8 cm stick down and lifts the other two from its ends. They do not even touch!
text: The two short sticks together are only 3 + 4 = 7 cm long. They cannot stretch across 8 cm. To make a triangle, the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side.
With 4 cm, 9 cm and 13 cm, the short sticks add to exactly 13. They lie flat on top of the long stick, and there is no triangle.

picture.caption: The two shorter sides must add to more than the longest side.

think.question: Can 6 cm, 7 cm and 12 cm make a triangle?

lessons.aha: Two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side.
formulas: a + b > c (c is the longest side)

lessons.title: How long can the third side be?
lessons.story: Anu has sticks of 6 cm and 9 cm. 'Which third stick can I use?' she asks.
text: If the third side is very short, the two sides almost close up: it must be more than 9 − 6 = 3 cm. If it is very long, the two sides almost lie flat: it must be less than 9 + 6 = 15 cm.
So the third side x must be between the difference and the sum: 3 cm < x < 15 cm.

picture.caption: The third side must lie strictly between 3 cm and 15 cm.

think.question: Two sides are 7 cm and 10 cm. Write the range of the third side.

lessons.aha: Difference < third side < sum.

lessons.title: Drawing a triangle exactly
lessons.story: The teacher asks for a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Ravi draws it 'by eye' and it looks wrong. Anu uses compasses.
text: Step 1: draw the base BC = 6 cm. Step 2: open the compasses to 5 cm, put the point on B and draw an arc. Step 3: open to 7 cm, put the point on C and draw another arc. Step 4: the arcs cross at A. Join AB and AC.
Each arc shows all the points that are a fixed distance from one end. Where the two arcs cross, A is at the right distance from both B and C.

picture.caption: Constructing a triangle from three sides.

think.question: Why must you keep the arcs on your drawing?
think.answer: They show the teacher how you found A; they earn marks.

lessons.aha: Draw the base, swing two arcs, join to where they cross.

lessons.title: Why the arcs work: circles
lessons.story: Anu ties a string to a pin and swings a pencil around it. She gets a circle. 'Every point on it is the same distance from the pin!'
text: All points at a fixed distance from a centre make a circle. An arc is a piece of that circle. So an arc of radius 5 cm from B shows every point that is 5 cm from B.
Equilateral triangle: draw AB, and draw arcs of radius AB from both A and B. The crossing point C is the same distance from A and B as AB itself, so all three sides are equal.

picture.caption: Arcs of the same radius from A and B meet at C: an equilateral triangle.

think.question: Two arcs of radius 3 cm are drawn from A and B, with AB = 8 cm. Do they meet?
think.answer: No: 3 + 3 = 6 < 8. This is the triangle rule again!

lessons.aha: An arc shows all points at one distance from its centre. Where two arcs cross, both distances are right.

lessons.title: Two sides and an angle, or two angles and a side
lessons.story: The teacher asks for triangle PQR with PQ = 5 cm, ∠Q = 60° and QR = 6 cm. Another triangle has ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 70° and AB = 6 cm.
text: Two sides and the angle between them (SAS): draw QR = 6 cm, make a 60° angle at Q, mark P on that arm at 5 cm, and join PR.
Two angles and the side between them (ASA): draw AB = 6 cm, make 50° at A and 70° at B. The two arms meet at C.
Do triangles always exist? No: angles of 100° and 90° add to 190°, which is more than 180°, so the arms never meet.

steps: Mark the other side, or let arms meet
picture.caption: Constructing with SAS or ASA.

think.question: Can a triangle have ∠A = 110° and ∠B = 75°?

lessons.aha: SAS: side, angle, side. ASA: angle, side, angle. Two angles must add to less than 180°.

lessons.title: The 180° secret
lessons.story: Anu tears the three corners off a paper triangle and puts them side by side. They make a perfect straight line. She tries a thin triangle and a fat triangle. It works every time!
text: A straight line is 180°, so the three angles of every triangle add up to 180°. (In Chapter 5 we proved this with a parallel line.)
So if you know two angles, you know the third. Angles in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 are 2x, 3x and 4x with 9x = 180°, so x = 20° and the angles are 40°, 60° and 80°.

think.question: Can a triangle have two right angles?
think.answer: No. 90° + 90° = 180° leaves 0° for the third angle.

lessons.aha: The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°.

lessons.title: Special triangles and the outside angle
lessons.story: Ravi extends one side of his triangle past the corner. A new angle appears outside. 'Is there a rule for this one too?'
text: The outside angle (exterior angle) and the inside angle next to it make a straight line, so they add to 180°. The three inside angles also add to 180°. So the exterior angle must equal the sum of the two far (interior opposite) angles.
In an isosceles triangle, the two equal sides have equal angles opposite them. In an equilateral triangle, all three angles are 60°.

right.title: Exterior angle
lines: = sum of the two far angles

picture.caption: Two quick rules that save time.

think.question: An exterior angle is 110° and one far angle is 45°. Find the other far angle.

lessons.aha: Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles. Equal sides face equal angles.

lessons.title: Altitudes: the height of a triangle
lessons.story: Ravi wants to know the height of his triangular kite. Thatha says, 'Drop a straight line from the top, at right angles to the bottom edge.'
text: An altitude is the perpendicular line from a vertex to the opposite side (or to that side extended). Every triangle has three altitudes, and they meet at one point.
In an obtuse triangle, two altitudes fall outside the triangle, so you must extend the sides. To construct one, use a set square or construct a perpendicular from the vertex.

picture.caption: The altitude from A meets BC at a right angle.

think.question: How many altitudes does a triangle have?

lessons.aha: An altitude is perpendicular to a side and passes through the opposite vertex.

Form an equation with the angle sum.

notes.subtitle: Multiplying & Dividing Fractions

concepts.title: A fraction of something
concepts.text: 'Of' means multiply. To find 2/5 of a quantity, divide by 5 and multiply by 2.

concepts.title: Fraction × fraction: a picture
concepts.text: Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. Cancel common factors first.

concepts.title: Mixed numbers
concepts.text: Always change mixed numbers into improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.

concepts.title: Dividing: how many fit?
concepts.text: To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: keep, change, flip.

method: Change mixed numbers to improper fractions.
Change 'of' to ×, and ÷ to × reciprocal.
Cancel common factors.
Simplify and write as a mixed number if needed.

practice.question: Find 3/8 of 64.
Reciprocal of 2 1/2.
How many 1/3 kg packets from 5 kg?
Find 2/3 of 3/4 of 120.
A tank holds 40 L. It is 3/5 full. How many litres more fill it?
A plot of 3 1/2 acres is shared equally by 4 brothers. Each gives 1/7 of his share to a school. How much does the school get?

notes.intro: Anu's mother bakes a cake and asks her to take 3/4 of the 2 cups of sugar. Then Thatha wants to cut a 12 m rope into pieces of 3/4 m. How much sugar? How many pieces?
before: change mixed numbers to improper fractions

lessons.title: A fraction of something
lessons.story: Mother says, 'Use 2/5 of the 45 sweets for the guests.' Anu wonders how many that is.
text: 2/5 means: cut into 5 equal parts and take 2 of them. 45 ÷ 5 = 9 in each part. 2 parts = 18 sweets.
In maths, 'of' means multiply: 2/5 of 45 = 2/5 × 45 = 90/5 = 18.

picture.caption: 45 sweets in 5 equal parts of 9. Two parts = 18.

think.question: How many minutes is 3/4 of 2 hours?

lessons.aha: 'Of' means multiply. To find 2/5 of a quantity, divide by 5 and multiply by 2.

lessons.title: Fraction × fraction: a picture
lessons.story: Anu has 2/3 of a chocolate bar. She gives 3/5 of her piece to Ravi. What part of the whole bar does Ravi get?
text: Draw a rectangle for the whole bar. Cut it into 3 rows and shade 2 rows (2/3). Cut it into 5 columns and take 3 columns (3/5). The overlap is 2 × 3 = 6 small boxes out of 3 × 5 = 15.
So 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15 = 2/5. The rule: multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms.

picture.caption: The gold boxes show 2/3 of 3/5: 6 out of 15.

lessons.aha: Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. Cancel common factors first.

lessons.title: Mixed numbers
lessons.story: Thatha's car runs 14 1/2 km on one litre of petrol. How far does it go on 6 3/4 litres?
text: Change each mixed number to an improper fraction first: 14 1/2 = 29/2 and 6 3/4 = 27/4.

picture.caption: Mixed → improper → multiply → back to mixed.

lessons.aha: Always change mixed numbers into improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.

lessons.title: Does multiplying always make bigger?
lessons.story: Ravi says, 'Multiplying always makes a number bigger.' Anu works out 10 × 1/2 = 5. 'It got smaller!'
text: Multiplying by a proper fraction (less than 1) gives a smaller answer: you take only a part. Multiplying by 1 gives the same number. Multiplying by an improper fraction (more than 1) gives a bigger answer.
Properties: a × b = b × a (order does not matter), (a × b) × c = a × (b × c), a × 1 = a and a × 0 = 0. These are true for fractions too.

picture.caption: × less than 1 → smaller; × more than 1 → bigger.

think.question: Without calculating, is 7/8 × 25 more or less than 25?

lessons.aha: × a number less than 1 makes smaller; × a number more than 1 makes bigger.

lessons.title: Dividing: how many fit?
lessons.story: Thatha cuts a 12 m rope into pieces of 3/4 m. 'How many pieces?' he asks.
text: Division asks how many times one quantity fits into another. Each metre gives 4 quarters, so 12 m has 48 quarters. Each piece uses 3 quarters, so there are 48 ÷ 3 = 16 pieces.
The quick rule: dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal (turn it upside down). 12 ÷ 3/4 = 12 × 4/3 = 16.

picture.caption: Each metre is 4 quarters; one piece uses 3 quarters.

think.question: How many 1/3 kg packets can be filled from 5 kg?

lessons.aha: To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: keep, change, flip.

lessons.title: Fraction word problems
lessons.story: Meena has ₹600. She spends 1/3 on books, then 1/4 of the remaining money on food. What fraction of ₹600 is left?
text: Read carefully: 'of the remaining money' means first find what is left. Books: 1/3 × 600 = ₹200, so ₹400 remains.

picture.caption: Take 1/3 of the whole, then 1/4 of what remains.

think.question: A recipe for 4 people needs 2/3 cup of sugar. How much for 6 people?

lessons.aha: Find the remaining amount first when a question says 'of the rest'.

lessons.title: Fractional relations
lessons.story: Ravi's height is 4/5 of Anu's height. Anu is 150 cm tall. How tall is Ravi? And Anu's height is what fraction of Ravi's?
text: If A is 4/5 of B, then B is 5/4 of A: flip the fraction. Check: 5/4 × 120 = 150. ✓

picture.caption: Ravi is 4 parts when Anu is 5 parts.

think.question: A is 2/3 of B, and A = 18. Find B.

lessons.aha: If A is p/q of B, then B is q/p of A.

examples.question: How many 3/4 m pieces from 12 m?
₹600: 1/3 on books, 1/4 of the rest on food. Fraction left?
2/3 cup sugar for 4 people. Sugar for 6 people?

mistakes: Adding denominators when multiplying.
Flipping the first fraction instead of the second.
Not changing mixed numbers to improper fractions.
Taking 'of the rest' of the original amount.
checklist: Write the answer in lowest terms.

notes.subtitle: Congruent Figures & Triangle Congruence

concepts.title: What congruent means
concepts.text: Congruent = same shape and same size. Write matching vertices in the same order.

concepts.title: Do we need all six measurements?
concepts.text: Three well-chosen matching parts are enough: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS or RHS.

concepts.title: Two traps: AAA and SSA
concepts.text: AAA and SSA do not prove congruence.

concepts.title: Writing a twin proof
concepts.text: Name the triangles, give three equal parts with reasons, name the condition, then use CPCT.

formulas: AAA and SSA do not prove congruence
method: Name the two triangles.
Write three pairs of equal parts with reasons.
State the condition.
Use CPCT for the result.

example.question: AB = PQ, BC = QR, ∠B = ∠Q.
steps: The angle is between the two sides.

practice.question: ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ. Write the side equal to BC.
Which condition: three sides equal?
Can AAA prove congruence?
ΔPQR ≅ ΔLMN, ∠P = 40°, ∠M = 75°. Find ∠N.
Isosceles triangle, base angle 50°. Find the vertex angle.
Name the condition: ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, BC = QR.
In ΔABC, AB = AC and ∠A = 40°. Find ∠B.
Prove that the diagonal of a square divides it into two congruent triangles.
practice.answer: SSS (or SAS) with the diagonal common

practice.question: Two triangles have sides 4, 5, 6 cm and 6, 4, 5 cm. Are they congruent?
AB = AC, D is the mid-point of BC. Prove that AD ⟂ BC.

tips: AAA gives the same shape only.
notes.intro: Anu finds two identical leaves on the ground and places one exactly on top of the other. They match perfectly. 'Twins!' she laughs. In mathematics, shapes that match exactly are called congruent.
before: know the angle sum of a triangle
know vertically opposite and alternate angles

lessons.title: What congruent means
lessons.story: Anu traces a stamp onto paper, cuts it out and places it on another stamp. Every edge matches.
text: Two figures are congruent if one can be placed exactly on the other: same shape and same size. We use the symbol ≅.
The order of letters matters. ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR means A matches P, B matches Q and C matches R. So AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP, and ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R.

picture.caption: Matching letters show matching parts.

think.question: If ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, which side equals BC?

lessons.aha: Congruent = same shape and same size. Write matching vertices in the same order.

lessons.title: Do we need all six measurements?
lessons.story: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 angles. Ravi says, 'To check twins, we must measure all six!' Thatha says, 'Three are enough, if you choose wisely.'
text: SSS: if all three sides match, the triangle is fixed, so the triangles are congruent. Try it with sticks: three fixed lengths make only one shape.
SAS: two sides and the angle between them. ASA: two angles and the side between them. AAS: two angles and any matching side. RHS: in right triangles, the hypotenuse and one side.

picture.caption: Five ways to prove two triangles congruent.

think.question: AB = PQ, BC = QR and ∠B = ∠Q. Which condition is this?
think.answer: SAS (the angle is between the two sides).

lessons.aha: Three well-chosen matching parts are enough: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS or RHS.

lessons.title: Two traps: AAA and SSA
lessons.story: Anu draws a small equilateral triangle and a big one. All their angles are 60°. 'Twins?' she asks.
text: No. Equal angles give the same shape but not the same size. So AAA does not prove congruence.
SSA (an angle that is NOT between the two sides) can also give two different triangles. So only use SAS when the angle is between the two sides.

picture.caption: Same angles, different sizes: not congruent.

think.question: Can AAA prove two triangles congruent?
think.answer: No. It only proves the same shape.

lessons.aha: AAA and SSA do not prove congruence.

lessons.title: Writing a twin proof
lessons.story: Quadrilateral ABCD looks like a kite: AB = AD and CB = CD. Thatha asks Anu to prove that ∠B = ∠D.
text: Draw the diagonal AC. Compare ΔABC and ΔADC: AB = AD (given), CB = CD (given), and AC = AC (common side).
So ΔABC ≅ ΔADC by SSS. Matching parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT), so ∠B = ∠D.

picture.caption: The four steps of a congruence proof.

think.question: What does CPCT stand for?
think.answer: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles (are equal).

lessons.aha: Name the triangles, give three equal parts with reasons, name the condition, then use CPCT.

lessons.title: Isosceles triangles
lessons.story: Ravi folds an isosceles triangle along the line from the top to the middle of the base. The two halves match exactly!
text: The fold line splits the triangle into two congruent triangles (SSS). So the two base angles match: angles opposite equal sides are equal.
If AB = AC and ∠B = 65°, then ∠C = 65° and ∠A = 180° − 130° = 50°.

picture.caption: AB = AC, so ∠B = ∠C.

think.question: An isosceles triangle has vertex angle 100°. Find the base angles.

lessons.aha: Equal sides face equal angles.

lessons.title: Twins in real life: why triangles are strong
lessons.story: Ravi makes a square and a triangle from straws and pins. He pushes the square: it squashes into a slanted shape. He pushes the triangle: it does not move at all!
text: By SSS, three fixed sides fix the whole triangle. Its shape cannot change. A square with fixed sides can still change its angles.
That is why bridges, roof trusses, electricity towers and bicycle frames are built from triangles. Factories also make congruent parts so that any spare part fits.

picture.caption: Triangles are rigid; squares are not.

think.question: How can you make a square frame rigid?
think.answer: Add a diagonal rod: it splits the square into two triangles.

lessons.aha: Three fixed sides fix a triangle completely. This makes triangles strong.

examples.question: AB = PQ, BC = QR, ∠B = ∠Q.
steps: The angle is between the two sides.

examples.question: Prove ∠B = ∠D in kite ABCD with AB = AD, CB = CD.
AB and CD bisect each other at O. Prove AC = BD.
Hypotenuse 10 cm and one side 6 cm in both.

mistakes: Using AAA as a congruence condition.
Writing vertices in the wrong order.
Using SAS when the angle is not between the sides.
Not giving reasons.

notes.subtitle: Multiplying & Dividing Integers

concepts.title: Numbers below zero
concepts.text: Right means bigger, left means smaller. Below zero, the numbers are negative.

concepts.title: Tokens: plus and minus cancel
concepts.text: A + and a − token make 0. Subtracting a negative means adding.

concepts.title: Multiplying with a negative
concepts.text: Positive × negative = negative.

concepts.title: Why negative × negative is positive
concepts.text: Same signs give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer.

method: Decide the sign first.
Then work with the sizes of the numbers.
Use the distributive property for smart calculation.
Check with a number-line picture.

practice.question: Find (−2)⁴.
Find (−1)⁹⁹.
A diver at −30 m goes down 4 m every minute for 5 minutes. Find the new depth.
Find 15 × (−8) + 15 × 18 using the distributive property.
A shop makes a profit of ₹40 on each pen and a loss of ₹15 on each notebook. It sells 30 pens and 50 notebooks. Find the net result.

notes.intro: Anu visits Shimla in winter. The temperature at noon is 5°C and at night it falls by 12°C. It goes below zero! You learn why negative × negative is positive, using patterns and tokens instead of just remembering a rule.
before: add and subtract integers on a number line
know that subtracting a negative is adding

lessons.title: The carrom coin game
lessons.story: Anu and Ravi play a game on a number line drawn on the carrom board. Forward moves are +, backward moves are −. The coin starts at 0 and moves +3, −5, then +4.
text: 0 + 3 = 3. Then 3 − 5 = −2 (it goes past zero). Then −2 + 4 = 2. The coin ends at 2.
The game shows that adding a negative number is the same as moving backward.

picture.caption: +3, −5, +4 takes the coin from 0 to 2.

think.question: Start at 1 and move −4, −3, +5. Where is the coin?

lessons.aha: Forward = add a positive number. Backward = add a negative number.

lessons.title: Numbers below zero
lessons.story: The thermometer shows 5°C. At night it drops 12 degrees. Anu counts down: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, … −7.
text: Integers are the whole numbers with their negatives: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, … On a number line, positive numbers go right and negative numbers go left.
Adding moves right; subtracting moves left. 5 − 12 = −7.

picture.caption: Starting at 5 and moving 12 steps left lands on −7.

think.question: The temperature is −3°C and rises by 8°C. What is it now?

lessons.aha: Right means bigger, left means smaller. Below zero, the numbers are negative.

lessons.title: Tokens: plus and minus cancel
lessons.story: Thatha gives Anu blue tokens (+1) and gold tokens (−1). 'A blue and a gold together make zero,' he says.
text: 5 blue and 3 gold: the 3 pairs cancel, and 2 blue remain. So 5 + (−3) = 2.
Subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive: 8 − (−7) = 8 + 7 = 15. Taking away a debt makes you richer!

picture.caption: 3 pairs of + and − cancel; +2 remains.

lessons.aha: A + and a − token make 0. Subtracting a negative means adding.

lessons.title: Multiplying with a negative
lessons.story: Anu loses ₹6 every day for 4 days. 'How much has my money changed?'
text: Losing ₹6 four times is (−6) + (−6) + (−6) + (−6) = −24. So 4 × (−6) = −24. A positive times a negative is negative.
Order does not matter in multiplication, so (−6) × 4 = −24 as well.

picture.caption: Four jumps of −6 land on −24.

lessons.aha: Positive × negative = negative.

lessons.title: Why negative × negative is positive
lessons.story: Ravi says, 'A minus times a minus giving a plus is just a rule to memorise.' Thatha says, 'No, there is a pattern. Watch.'
text: Look at this column: (−6) × 2 = −12, (−6) × 1 = −6, (−6) × 0 = 0. Each time the second number goes down by 1, the answer goes UP by 6.
Continue the pattern: (−6) × (−1) = 6, (−6) × (−2) = 12. So negative × negative is positive. With many factors, count the negatives: even count → positive, odd count → negative.

picture.caption: The answers go up by 6 each step, so they become positive.

lessons.aha: Same signs give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer.

lessons.title: Brahmagupta's rules: fortune and debt
lessons.story: About 1,400 years ago, in 628 CE, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for positive and negative numbers. He called positive numbers 'fortunes' and negative numbers 'debts'.
text: His rules: fortune × fortune = fortune. Debt × debt = fortune. Fortune × debt = debt. Division follows the same rules.
He also wrote that a number minus itself is zero, and that a debt subtracted from zero becomes a fortune: 0 − (−5) = 5. These are the same rules we use today.

picture.caption: Brahmagupta's sign rules for × and ÷.

think.question: Use the rules: (−12) ÷ (−3).

lessons.aha: Same signs give a positive result. Different signs give a negative result.

lessons.title: Division is multiplication backwards
lessons.story: Ravi asks, 'Why is (−48) ÷ 6 = −8?' Anu answers with a multiplication.
text: Division asks: what times 6 gives −48? Since 6 × (−8) = −48, the answer is −8. Every division fact comes from a multiplication fact.
0 ÷ 5 = 0, because 5 × 0 = 0. But 5 ÷ 0 has no answer: no number times 0 gives 5. So division by 0 is not defined.

picture.caption: Each division fact is a multiplication fact read backwards.

think.question: Find (−56) ÷ (−7) and check with multiplication.

lessons.aha: a ÷ b = c means b × c = a. Division by 0 is not possible.

lessons.title: Rules that never change
lessons.story: Anu notices that 3 + (−7) = (−7) + 3 and (−2) × 5 = 5 × (−2). 'Can I always swap?' she asks.
text: For + and ×, you can swap the order (commutative) and change the grouping (associative): (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). Also a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c (distributive).
For − and ÷, you cannot swap: 5 − 3 = 2 but 3 − 5 = −2.
Special numbers: a + 0 = a, a × 1 = a, a × 0 = 0, a × (−1) = −a, and a + (−a) = 0.

picture.caption: Properties of operations on integers.

lessons.aha: Swap and regroup freely for + and ×, never for − and ÷.

lessons.title: A magic grid of integers
lessons.story: Thatha gives Anu a 3 × 3 grid. 'Use the numbers −4 to 4, once each, so that every row, column and diagonal adds to 0.'
text: The total of −4 to 4 is 0, so each of the 3 rows must add to 0 ÷ 3 = 0. The centre must be the middle number, 0.
A quick way: take the 1-to-9 magic square and subtract 5 from every number. Every line had sum 15, and now each line loses 3 × 5 = 15, so every sum becomes 0.

picture.caption: Every row, column and diagonal adds to 0.

think.question: Add 2 to every number in this grid. What is the new magic sum?
think.answer: Each line gains 3 × 2 = 6, so the sum is 6.

lessons.aha: Adding the same number to every cell keeps a magic square magic.

lessons.title: Dividing integers and real-life problems
lessons.story: In a quiz, a correct answer gets +5 and a wrong answer gets −2. Ravi has 8 correct and 6 wrong. What is his score?
text: Division follows the same sign rules as multiplication: (−48) ÷ (−6) = 8 and (−48) ÷ 6 = −8. Never divide by 0: it has no answer.

picture.caption: +40 for correct answers, −12 for wrong ones: the score is 28.

think.question: A submarine at −120 m rises 40 m every minute. When does it reach the surface?

lessons.aha: Division uses the same sign rules. Division by zero is not allowed.

mistakes: Thinking (−)(−) is negative.
Treating 8 − (−7) as 1.
Saying a number ÷ 0 = 0.
Counting negative signs wrongly in long products.
checklist: Write the sign rule you use.
Check the sign at the end.
